summary: Discourages introducing software defects, in general and in network protocol implementations specifically. It notes that defects are among the largest cost drivers in networking and clarifies best current practice. It is informational and widely understood as a lighthearted piece.

plainLanguage.summary: Please do not put bugs in your programs on purpose, because bugs cost a lot.

subtitle: A humorous call to stop introducing bugs into software.

tldr.problem: Software bugs are extremely costly and cause numerous failures and degradations across systems. The problem seems obvious yet persists.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9225 proposes a straightforward solution: implementers must not introduce bugs when writing software. It outlines best practices for avoiding, documenting, and handling defects.
tldr.outcome: This April Fools' joke takes a deadpan approach to stating the obvious, while also noting real examples of billion-dollar bugs and the genuine economic cost of software defects.

today: RFC 9225 is an Informational RFC published on April 1, 2022. It remains the lighthearted but pointed reminder that software defects are harmful and should be avoided.

sections.title: The Case Against Bugs
sections.content: RFC 9225 is an April Fools' RFC that discourages the practice of introducing software defects. The document takes a humorous, deadpan tone while making the obvious point: implementers MUST NOT introduce bugs when writing software. Software defects are errors, flaws, or faults that cause programs to produce incorrect or unexpected results.
sections.plainLanguage: Bugs are mistakes in programs. The joke is that someone needed to write an official RFC to tell people not to make mistakes on purpose.

sections.title: Real Examples of Expensive Bugs
sections.content: The RFC describes several real-world examples where software defects led to catastrophic failures. The Ariane 5 rocket failure in 1996 cost billions in development but was destroyed 40 seconds after launch due to a data conversion bug. The NASA Deep Impact spacecraft was rendered inoperable by a fault in its fault-protection software. A 1983 Soviet early warning satellite misclassified clouds as missile launches. A NIST study found that programming bugs cost the U.S. economy about 0.6 percent of gross domestic product annually, with each person working roughly an hour per week to compensate for buggy software.
sections.plainLanguage: Bugs have cost real money and caused real problems: rockets that exploded, satellites that broke, and money wasted because of mistakes in programs.

sections.title: Best Current Practices
sections.content: The RFC proposes six best practices. Developers must not implement bugs. If bugs are introduced, they must be clearly documented. For broken specifications, it is recommended to aggregate multiple smaller bugs into one larger, easier-to-recognize bug. The phrase "it is not a bug, it is a feature" is considered rude. All external input should be assumed to result from bugs, and the same applies to internal inputs. The document notes that improving the security posture requires a thorough review of existing software to find remaining bugs.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC's main advice: do not make bugs on purpose. If bugs happen, write down what they are. Treat any unexpected input as if it came from a bug.
